topics.title: The financial system
topics.detail: A financial system is the network that moves money from people or organisations with surplus funds to those who need funds.
topics.simple: Think of it as the economy's money-connection system: savers, borrowers, markets, institutions and regulators all connect through it.
topics.example: A household saves money in a bank. The bank lends to a business that needs funds to buy equipment. The system connects the saver and borrower.
points: It includes financial markets, institutions, instruments and services, with regulators supervising the system.
topics.key: Markets enable issue and trading; institutions collect, lend, invest and insure; instruments are products such as shares and bonds; regulators supervise participants.

topics.title: Financial markets and their functions
topics.detail: Financial markets are systems where financial assets are created, issued and traded.
topics.simple: A market connects buyers and sellers and helps establish a price for financial products.
topics.example: An investor sells listed shares to another investor through the secondary market.
points: Functions include price discovery, liquidity, lower transaction/information costs, savings mobilisation, diversification and transferability.
topics.key: Primary markets issue new securities; secondary markets trade existing securities. Liquidity means being able to sell without a major price impact.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Money market instruments are short-term and generally mature within 365 days. The handwritten notes contrast CDs as wholesale in nature with FDs as generally retail. Call money is very short-term funding used when money is needed immediately; a rise in call-money rates can signal tight short-term liquidity.

topics.title: Financial institutions
topics.detail: Financial institutions are organisations that help people and businesses save, borrow, invest, insure and make payments.
topics.simple: They are the organisations doing the work inside the financial system.
topics.example: A commercial bank accepts deposits and provides loans. A mutual fund pools investors' money and invests it.
points: The material covers commercial banks, co-operative banks, payment banks, small finance banks, NBFCs, ARCs, primary dealers, DFIs, mutual funds, insurers and pension funds.
topics.key: Payment banks can accept eligible deposits and facilitate payments but cannot lend. Small finance banks can accept deposits and lend. NBFCs do not have all banking powers.
topics.classNotes: Class note: The notes distinguish neobanks (for example, Jupiter) from banks with physical branches. They also compare factoring and forfaiting as receivables-finance arrangements; the exact distinction depends on the tenor and nature of the receivable, so check the lecture wording before using it in an exam answer.

topics.title: Financial services
topics.detail: Financial services are specialist activities that help raise funds, invest, trade, safeguard assets and complete transactions.
topics.simple: Think of them as the support services that make financial markets work.
topics.example: An investment banker coordinates a company's IPO; a registrar processes applications; a custodian safeguards securities.
points: The slides cover investment/merchant banking, distribution, advisory, credit rating, custody, factoring, forfaiting, leasing, hire purchase and housing finance.
topics.key: Factoring usually involves short-term receivables. Forfaiting is described as non-recourse purchase of export receivables, generally medium/long term.
topics.classNotes: Class note: The handwritten pages also mention bill discounting, factoring, forfaiting, export credit and letters of credit. These are trade-finance tools: they help a seller receive funds earlier or help a buyer/seller manage payment risk.

topics.title: Early-stage funding
topics.detail: Start-ups need money before their product or business model is fully proven.
topics.simple: A business idea often needs funding before it earns enough to pay its own bills.
topics.example: A start-up uses seed funding to build a prototype, test demand and hire its first team.
points: Pre-seed/seed supports an idea or prototype; early stage follows proof of concept; later stage supports growth and scaling.
topics.key: Sources include founders, friends/family, angel investors, venture capital, crowdfunding and incubators/accelerators.

topics.title: Angel investors, venture capital and private equity
topics.detail: Angel investors and VCs invest in young businesses with growth potential; PE generally focuses on more mature businesses.
topics.simple: An angel may invest personal money early. A VC fund invests professionally in start-ups. A PE investor usually invests later in a business with a track record.
topics.example: A VC evaluates market size, scalability, product, promoter, technology and risks before investing.
points: VC process: deal origination, screening, evaluation, negotiation, post-investment monitoring and exit. Exit may occur through IPO, acquisition, buy-back or sale.
topics.key: Post-money valuation = pre-money valuation + new investment. Investor ownership is investment divided by post-money valuation.

topics.title: IPO process
topics.detail: An IPO is a public offer by an unlisted company seeking to list its securities on a stock exchange.
topics.simple: A company that was privately held offers shares to public investors for the first time.
topics.example: Company appoints intermediaries, completes due diligence, files DRHP, responds to review, announces price band, receives bids, allots shares and lists.
points: Key intermediaries include lead manager/BRLM, registrar, bankers to issue, underwriters, syndicate members, depositories and DPs.
topics.key: DRHP is the draft offer document. Registrar processes applications and allotment. After listing, shares trade in the secondary market.

topics.title: Book building
topics.detail: Book building collects investor bids within a price band to help determine an IPO's final issue price.
topics.simple: Instead of fixing the final price first, the issuer asks investors what price and quantity they are willing to bid for.
topics.example: In the class illustration, 3,000 shares are offered from ₹20–₹24. Bids are 500 at ₹24, 1,000 at ₹23 and 1,500 at ₹22; demand reaches 3,000 at ₹22.
points: Fixed-price issues announce a price in advance. Book building uses a price band and demand schedule.
topics.key: Cut-off is the price at which the offered quantity is met in the classroom demand schedule.

topics.title: ASBA
topics.detail: ASBA means Applications Supported by Blocked Amount. IPO application money stays blocked in the bank account until allotment.
topics.simple: You apply for shares but the bank does not immediately take the money out of your account.
topics.example: If ₹15,000 is blocked and shares worth ₹6,000 are allotted, ₹6,000 is debited and the remaining amount is unblocked.
points: SCSBs are banks designated to provide ASBA services.
topics.key: Only the allotted amount is debited; unused blocked money is released.

topics.title: Secondary market
topics.detail: The secondary market is where already-issued securities are traded between investors.
topics.simple: The company has already issued the share. Now investors buy and sell it among themselves.
topics.example: You buy a listed share from another investor through the exchange; the company does not receive the sale proceeds.
points: Secondary markets support liquidity, price discovery, market participation and monitoring.
topics.key: Bid is buyer's price; ask is seller's price; LTP is the latest completed trade price, not a guaranteed execution price.

topics.title: Market, limit and stop-loss orders
topics.detail: An order tells the broker how you want to buy or sell a security.
topics.simple: Different order types trade off speed, price control and trigger conditions.
topics.example: A buy limit at ₹100 means buy at ₹100 or lower, but it may not execute. A market order seeks immediate execution but price can vary.
points: Market order prioritises execution. Limit order sets an acceptable price. Stop-loss activates an order when its trigger price is reached.
topics.key: Market order: execution not price certainty. Limit order: price control not execution certainty. Stop trigger does not guarantee execution at that exact price.
topics.classNotes: Class note — order practice: a buy limit order at ₹4,300 will not execute immediately if the market is ₹4,400; it can execute only at ₹4,300 or lower. A buy stop is a trigger order: if the trigger is ₹730, it activates when the market reaches the trigger, with execution depending on the order type and available price. A stop-loss sell with trigger ₹1,510 and limit ₹1,500 becomes a limit sell after the trigger; it is not guaranteed to execute.

topics.title: Equity shares
topics.detail: An equity share represents ownership in a company.
topics.simple: Buying a share means owning a small part of the company.
topics.example: A company may reinvest profits rather than pay dividends; shareholders may benefit from future growth but dividends are not guaranteed.
points: Equity holders have voting rights as specified and a residual claim after creditors in liquidation.
topics.key: Dividend yield = annual dividend per share ÷ market price per share × 100. The slides classify stocks by size, dividends, fundamentals, risk and economic cycle.

topics.title: Bond basics
topics.detail: A bond is a loan made by an investor to an issuer. The issuer promises interest and repayment of principal according to the terms.
topics.simple: You lend money to a government or company and receive interest if payments are made as promised.
topics.example: A ₹1,000 bond with a 7% annual coupon pays ₹70 annually if the terms specify annual payments.
points: Key terms: face value, coupon rate, coupon payment, maturity, market price, premium/discount and yield.
topics.key: Debt investors are creditors; equity investors are owners. Creditors generally rank ahead of shareholders in insolvency.

topics.title: Bond valuation
topics.detail: A bond's price is the present value of its future coupon payments plus the present value of principal repayment.
topics.simple: Work out what all future bond payments are worth today, using the required market yield.
topics.example: A ₹1,000 bond paying a 7% annual coupon for five years is worth about ₹960.51 at an 8% required yield in the class example.
points: P = C × [1 − (1+y)^(-n)] ÷ y + FV ÷ (1+y)^n. C=coupon per period; y=yield per period; n=periods; FV=face value.
topics.key: Market yields rise → existing fixed-coupon bond prices generally fall. For semi-annual bonds halve annual coupon/yield and double periods.
topics.classNotes: Class note — valuation method: discount every coupon separately and discount face value at maturity, then add the present values. For semi-annual coupons, convert the annual coupon and annual yield into per-period amounts and double the number of periods. The notes work through a ₹1,000 face-value bond with a 9% annual coupon, five years to maturity and a 10% required yield; the approximate value is ₹962.07 when coupons are annual.

topics.title: Yield to maturity
topics.detail: YTM is the return implied by the bond's current price if held to maturity and promised cash flows are received.
topics.simple: It combines coupon income and any gain or loss between the price paid and the amount repaid at maturity.
topics.example: A bond with a 7% coupon can have an 8% YTM if it trades at a discount.
points: YTM is the discount rate that makes PV of all future cash flows equal current market price.
topics.key: Coupon rate is calculated on face value; YTM depends on current market price and future cash flows.
topics.classNotes: Class note: YTM is the discount rate that equates the present value of all promised coupon and principal cash flows with the current market price. The handwritten examples also distinguish current yield (annual coupon ÷ current market price × 100) from YTM. For a callable bond, compare yield to call with YTM; the notes indicate choosing the more conservative/higher yield convention where required by the question.

topics.title: Macaulay and modified duration
topics.detail: Duration measures the weighted timing of bond cash flows and helps estimate interest-rate sensitivity.
topics.simple: It is not simply the maturity date. It tells you how sensitive the bond price may be when yields change.
topics.example: If modified duration is 4.16, a one-percentage-point rise in yield suggests an approximate 4.16% price fall.
points: Macaulay duration = sum of time × PV of cash flow divided by bond price. Modified duration = Macaulay duration ÷ (1 + yield per coupon period).
topics.key: Higher modified duration generally means greater price sensitivity. Convexity describes curvature in the price-yield relationship.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time at which the bond's present-value cash flows are received. Modified duration estimates price sensitivity: approximate percentage price change ≈ − modified duration × change in yield. The lecture also notes that higher duration generally means greater price sensitivity, all else equal.

topics.title: Treasury bill and discount yield
topics.detail: A discount instrument is bought below face value and redeemed at face value; the discount is the investor's return.
topics.simple: Pay ₹98 today and receive ₹100 at maturity. The ₹2 difference is the return before annualising.
topics.example: ₹100 face value CP bought for ₹98 with 91 days to maturity: effective yield ≈ (2/98) × (365/91) × 100 = 8.19%.
points: Effective yield uses purchase price in the denominator. Bank discount yield uses face value in the denominator.
topics.key: Effective yield = [(FV−price)/price] × (365/days) × 100. Bank discount yield = [(FV−price)/FV] × (365/days) × 100.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Keep the denominator straight. Effective yield uses the purchase price; bank discount yield uses face value. The handwritten notes introduce money-market instruments alongside this topic and emphasise the short maturity of money-market claims.

topics.title: Prospect Theory and loss aversion
topics.detail: People often feel the pain of losing money more strongly than the pleasure of gaining the same amount.
topics.simple: A ₹100 loss can feel worse than a ₹100 gain feels good.
topics.example: An investor may sell a small winner quickly but hold a losing share hoping it returns to the purchase price.
points: People judge outcomes relative to a reference point and respond differently to perceived gains and losses.
topics.key: The slides connect loss aversion with risk aversion and the disposition effect.

topics.title: Grossman–Stiglitz theory
topics.detail: If markets were perfectly efficient, investors would have little reason to pay to gather information.
topics.simple: Research costs money. If all useful information were already reflected in prices, why would anyone do the research?
topics.example: Informed investors research mispriced securities and trade; their trading helps prices move towards information-based values.
points: Because information is costly, perfectly efficient markets cannot be sustained all the time.
topics.key: The slides compare this to people repairing weak spots in a bridge: the repair effort helps keep the bridge strong.

topics.title: Mental accounting
topics.detail: People mentally divide money into separate buckets and treat each bucket differently.
topics.simple: A rupee from salary and a rupee from a bonus are still both rupees, even if people behave differently with them.
topics.example: Someone may be cautious with salary but take bigger risks with a bonus because it feels like extra money.
points: Separate mental buckets can distort spending, saving and investment decisions.
topics.key: The slides suggest judging all money as one combined pool against overall financial goals.

topics.title: Disposition effect
topics.detail: The disposition effect is the tendency to sell winning investments too early and hold losing investments too long.
topics.simple: People like locking in a gain but find it uncomfortable to admit a loss.
topics.example: An investor sells a share after a small gain but refuses to sell another share that has fallen, hoping it will recover.
points: The slides link it to loss aversion, cognitive dissonance and mental accounting.
topics.key: Review the investment case and whole portfolio rather than focusing only on the purchase price.

topics.title: Mutual funds
topics.detail: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it according to a stated objective.
topics.simple: Many people contribute to one pool; a professional manager invests the pool and investors hold units.
topics.example: An equity fund combines investors' money to buy a portfolio of shares.
points: Income and gains are shared in proportion to units after expenses and levies.
topics.key: Funds may invest in equities, bonds, money-market instruments or other permitted securities. Returns are not guaranteed.

topics.title: NAV — Net Asset Value
topics.detail: NAV is the value of one mutual-fund unit.
topics.simple: Take everything the fund owns, subtract what it owes, and divide the result by the number of units.
topics.example: Securities ₹10.5m + cash ₹2m − liabilities ₹0.5m = net assets ₹12m. With 1m units, NAV = ₹12.
points: NAV per unit = (market value investments + other assets + accrued income − liabilities − accrued expenses) ÷ outstanding units.
topics.key: Use current market values, add receivables, deduct accrued expenses and use the correct units outstanding for the valuation date.
topics.classNotes: Class note — NAV workflow: add market value of investments and other assets, include accrued income where relevant, subtract liabilities and accrued expenses, then divide by units outstanding. The handwritten examples include dividends, ex-dividend NAV, reinvestment at the ex-dividend NAV and revised unit counts. Do not subtract a dividend twice: adjust NAV and units consistently with the scheme's stated treatment.

topics.title: NAV numerical adjustments
topics.detail: NAV questions require you to identify every asset and liability at the correct date, then divide by the correct unit count.
topics.simple: Do not just add the investment values. Include income due, expenses owed and updated units.
topics.example: If an investment falls 20%, use 80% of its value. Deduct an accrued fee once. If units are redeemed, use the new unit count.
points: The practice file includes fees, units, dividend reinvestment, growth, dividend yield, purchases, sales and cash flows.
topics.key: Net assets = assets − liabilities. NAV = net assets ÷ units outstanding. Watch the timing of each transaction.
topics.classNotes: Class note — dividend/reinvestment: the pages show a cum-dividend NAV, an ex-dividend NAV after the distribution, and reinvestment of the dividend amount into additional units at the ex-dividend NAV. Holding-period return is calculated as (final value − initial investment) ÷ initial investment × 100; include cash distributions if they were paid out rather than reinvested.

topics.title: Total Expense Ratio
topics.detail: TER is the recurring cost of operating a mutual fund, expressed as a percentage of assets.
topics.simple: It is the fund's running cost. Costs reduce the return left for investors.
topics.example: A fund earns a gross return, but management and operating expenses reduce the amount reflected in NAV.
points: The slides list management, distribution, audit, custodian, registration, communication and other scheme expenses.
topics.key: NAVs are reported net of expenses. Check the scheme documents for actual charges.

topics.title: Mutual fund structure
topics.detail: A mutual fund has several entities with different responsibilities.
topics.simple: The AMC manages the money, but other organisations safeguard assets, keep investor records and supervise the AMC.
topics.example: The custodian safeguards securities; the RTA processes applications and redemptions; trustees oversee the AMC.
points: The slides cover sponsor, trustees, AMC, custodian, RTA, fund accountant and auditor.
topics.key: Sponsor establishes the structure; trustees protect unit holders; AMC manages investments; custodian safekeeps securities.

topics.title: Mutual fund categories
topics.detail: A scheme category tells you what kind of assets or strategy a mutual fund focuses on.
topics.simple: Different funds invest in different things; the label gives you a starting point for understanding risk and portfolio.
topics.example: An equity fund invests mainly in shares; a liquid fund invests in very short-term debt; a hybrid fund combines asset classes.
points: The slides classify equity, debt, hybrid, solution-oriented and other schemes, including index funds, ETFs and FoFs.
topics.key: Equity funds carry equity-market risk; debt funds carry interest-rate and credit risk; hybrid funds combine exposures.

topics.title: SIP, SWP and STP
topics.detail: SIP puts money in regularly; SWP takes money out regularly; STP transfers money between schemes in stages.
topics.simple: SIP = invest. SWP = withdraw. STP = transfer.
topics.example: A monthly SIP invests ₹1,000. A retiree may use an SWP for regular withdrawals. An STP can move a lump sum gradually from a liquid fund to an equity fund.
points: SIP supports regular investing; SWP creates scheduled withdrawals; STP moves money from one scheme to another.
topics.key: Rupee-cost averaging can change average purchase cost but does not guarantee profit.

topics.title: Tracking error
topics.detail: Tracking error measures how closely an index fund follows its benchmark.
topics.simple: It measures how much the fund's return differs from the index over time.
topics.example: If the index returns 2% and the fund returns 1.8%, the difference for that period is −0.2 percentage points.
points: Periodic difference = fund return − benchmark return. Annualised tracking error = standard deviation of periodic differences × square root of periods per year.
topics.key: Slides use √12 for monthly data and √252 for daily data. Fees, cash, transaction costs and flows can create tracking differences.
topics.classNotes: Class note — calculation sequence: calculate each period's active return (fund return − benchmark return), find the mean active return, calculate deviations from that mean, square and sum them, divide by n−1 for sample variance, take the square root for monthly tracking error, then annualise by multiplying by √12. The handwritten worked examples use monthly observations.

topics.title: Portfolio construction
topics.detail: Portfolio construction is selecting and combining assets to fit goals, risk tolerance, liquidity and time horizon.
topics.simple: It is deciding what goes into the investment basket and how much of each thing to hold.
topics.example: A portfolio may combine shares from different sectors, bonds and cash instead of depending on one company.
points: The guide covers value, quality, factors, swing pricing and side pocketing.
topics.key: Diversification can reduce concentration risk but cannot eliminate broad market risk.

topics.title: Value investing
topics.detail: Value investors look for securities they believe are priced below their estimated fundamental worth.
topics.simple: They try to buy something for less than what they think it is worth.
topics.example: A learner compares a company's share price with earnings, book value, cash flow, debt and outlook.
points: The guide mentions P/E, P/B, dividend yield and free cash flow.
topics.key: Intrinsic value is an estimate, not a guaranteed price. An apparently cheap share may be cheap for a reason.

topics.title: Quality investing
topics.detail: Quality investing focuses on businesses with strong financial health and durable advantages.
topics.simple: Look for companies that are financially strong and can sustain their business.
topics.example: One company may have lower debt, stable profits and stronger cash generation than a similar competitor.
points: The guide highlights high ROE, low debt, stable earnings, strong cash flow and durable competitive advantage.
topics.key: A good company is not automatically a good investment at any price.

topics.title: Factor investing
topics.detail: Factor investing groups securities by characteristics linked to patterns in risk and return.
topics.simple: Instead of choosing only by company name, investors use characteristics such as value, momentum or quality.
topics.example: A momentum strategy may focus on securities with stronger recent price trends.
points: The guide lists value, momentum, size, quality, low volatility and growth.
topics.key: Value = inexpensive; momentum = recent trend; size = company size; quality = financial strength; low volatility = steadier price movement.

topics.title: Swing pricing
topics.detail: Swing pricing adjusts a fund's NAV during large inflows or outflows so the investors causing trading costs bear more of them.
topics.simple: If many people leave and the fund has to sell assets, the cost should not unfairly fall on only the investors who stay.
topics.example: Large redemptions can force a fund to trade and incur costs; an NAV adjustment aims to allocate those costs more fairly.
points: The guide gives an illustrative NAV adjustment from ₹100 to ₹98.
topics.key: It is intended to reduce dilution for continuing investors; actual application depends on scheme rules.

topics.title: Side pocketing
topics.detail: Side pocketing separates an illiquid or hard-to-value asset from the main portfolio.
topics.simple: Put the difficult-to-sell investment in a separate pocket so it does not distort the liquid part of the fund.
topics.example: If a bond becomes difficult to sell or value, it may be segregated while the main portfolio continues operating.
points: Investors present at segregation retain entitlement to recovery from the side pocket; new investors are not exposed to that isolated asset.
topics.key: Recovery is uncertain. The technique separates valuation/liquidity issues rather than making the loss disappear.

topics.title: Derivatives
topics.detail: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on another asset, called the underlying.
topics.simple: Its value is derived from something else: a share, index, currency, rate or commodity.
topics.example: A futures contract on an index changes value as the index/futures price changes.
points: The slides introduce forwards, futures, options, swaps and swaptions.
topics.key: Derivatives can be used for hedging, speculation and arbitrage.

topics.title: Forward contracts
topics.detail: A forward is a private agreement today to buy or sell an asset at an agreed price on a future date.
topics.simple: Two parties customise a deal now and promise to complete it later.
topics.example: A jeweller agrees to buy 15 kg of gold in three months at ₹2,450 per gram. If market price rises, the jeweller benefits; if it falls, the agreed price still applies.
points: Forwards are OTC and can be customised for quantity, quality, price and date. Both sides are obligated.
topics.key: Risks include counterparty default, low liquidity and rigidity.
topics.classNotes: Class note: The lecture's futures/forwards section uses long position for a buyer of the contract and short position for a seller. A long benefits when the futures price rises; a short benefits when it falls. Both sides are obligated under a forward, unlike an option buyer.

topics.title: Futures contracts
topics.detail: A future is a standardised agreement traded on an exchange to buy or sell an underlying at a predetermined price/date.
topics.simple: Like a forward, but standardised and exchange-traded.
topics.example: Buy 100 futures at 8,350 and exit at 8,475: profit = 100 × 125 = ₹12,500 before costs.
points: Futures specify lot size and expiry, require margin and can generally be closed by an opposite trade.
topics.key: Long benefits from rising prices; short benefits from falling prices. Open interest counts outstanding contracts once.
topics.classNotes: Class note — futures P/L: for a long futures position, gross P/L per unit = closing/exit futures price − entry futures price. For a short position, reverse the subtraction. Deduct transaction costs on the relevant legs. One handwritten SBI illustration uses entry ₹269.80, expiry/closing ₹275 and ₹0.20 transaction cost per unit, giving ₹5 net per unit or ₹5,000 for 1,000 units under that illustration's stated cost assumption.

topics.title: Futures margin and leverage
topics.detail: Margin is money deposited to support a futures position; it is only a fraction of the contract's full value.
topics.simple: You put down a deposit but your gains and losses are based on a much larger position.
topics.example: Contract value ₹835,000 at 15% margin requires ₹125,250 margin.
points: Initial margin = SPAN margin + exposure margin, as described in the slides.
topics.key: Leverage magnifies both gains and losses. Margin is not the maximum possible loss.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Margin is a performance deposit, not the purchase price of the underlying. The pages distinguish initial margin from mark-to-market settlement and note that leverage makes gains and losses large relative to the margin deposited.

topics.title: Mark-to-market
topics.detail: Futures positions are revalued each day and daily gains/losses are credited/debited.
topics.simple: Every trading day, the exchange works out how much the position gained or lost since the previous reference price.
topics.example: A long 2,000-unit position moves from ₹165 to ₹168.30: daily M2M = (168.30−165)×2,000 = ₹6,600 gain.
points: Daily M2M for a long = (today's close − previous reference price) × quantity.
topics.key: Maintain a running margin balance and compare it with initial/maintenance margin as required by the question.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Mark-to-market settles the daily gain or loss on an open futures position. A long position gains when the settlement price rises and loses when it falls; a short position behaves in the opposite way. Margin may need replenishment after adverse daily movements.

topics.title: Cost of carry and fair futures price
topics.detail: Futures pricing reflects spot price, financing cost, income from holding the asset and time to expiry.
topics.simple: Holding the underlying has costs and sometimes benefits; those affect the fair futures price.
topics.example: The class example uses spot Nifty 1,150, financing 11%, dividend yield 1% and one month to expiry, giving an illustrative futures price near 1,159.
points: Simplified slide formula: F = S × [1 + (r − d)]^t; S=spot, r=financing rate, d=dividend yield, t=time in years.
topics.key: Financing cost generally raises fair futures price; income such as dividends can reduce it.

topics.title: Options: calls and puts
topics.detail: An option buyer pays a premium for a right, not an obligation. The seller receives premium and takes on an obligation if exercised.
topics.simple: The buyer gets a choice; the seller has to fulfil the contract if the buyer uses that choice.
topics.example: A call gives the right to buy at strike. A put gives the right to sell at strike.
points: Strike price is the agreed exercise price; premium is the option price paid by buyer.
topics.key: Call buyer = right to buy. Put buyer = right to sell. Long option pays premium; short option receives premium.
topics.classNotes: Class note: An option buyer pays a premium for a right, not an obligation. A call gives the right to buy; a put gives the right to sell. The option seller/writer receives the premium and takes on the corresponding obligation if exercised.

topics.title: Option payoff and moneyness
topics.detail: Option payoff is the exercise value at expiry; net profit/loss also includes the premium.
topics.simple: First work out whether exercising has value. Then include the premium paid or received.
topics.example: Long call net P/L = max(S−K,0)−premium. Long put net P/L = max(K−S,0)−premium.
points: Call ITM if S>K; put ITM if S<K. Time value = premium − intrinsic value.
topics.key: Do not confuse payoff with net P/L. A buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Intrinsic value is the immediate exercise value; time value is the portion of premium above intrinsic value. A call is in-the-money when market price is above strike; a put is in-the-money when market price is below strike. At-the-money means market price and strike are equal (or very close, depending on the convention used).

topics.title: Option strategies
topics.detail: An option strategy combines positions to express a market view or manage risk.
topics.simple: Break the strategy into separate legs, calculate each leg, then add them together.
topics.example: Bull call spread buys a lower-strike call and sells a higher-strike call. The short call reduces cost but caps upside.
points: Covered call = long stock + short call. Protective put = long stock + long put. Bull call spread = long lower call + short higher call. Bear put spread = long higher put + short lower put.
topics.key: Always include premiums. State break-even, maximum gain and maximum loss where relevant.
topics.classNotes: Class note — strategy identification: covered call = long underlying + short call; protective put = long underlying + long put; bull call spread = buy lower-strike call and sell higher-strike call; bear put spread = buy higher-strike put and sell lower-strike put. The notes stress that a spread has two option legs and its payoff must be calculated by combining both legs with the net premium.

topics.title: Covered call
topics.detail: A covered call means owning shares and selling a call option against them.
topics.simple: You collect premium but agree to sell the shares at the strike if the option is exercised.
topics.example: Class example: 500 Reliance shares at ₹2,400; short call strike ₹2,500; premium ₹45. Break-even ₹2,355; maximum gain ₹145 per share under the example's one-to-one assumption.
points: Net P/L combines share P/L, short-call payoff and premium received.
topics.key: Upside is capped above strike; share downside remains, cushioned by premium.
topics.classNotes: Class note: A covered call is used when the investor already owns the underlying and sells a call to collect premium. The premium cushions a limited fall, but upside is capped above the strike because the short call may be exercised.

topics.title: Protective put
topics.detail: A protective put means owning shares and buying a put to protect against a fall.
topics.simple: The put acts like insurance: if the share falls below strike, the put gains value.
topics.example: Class example: Infosys purchase price ₹1,500; put strike ₹1,480; premium ₹40. Break-even ₹1,540 and maximum loss ₹60 per share.
points: Net P/L = stock P/L + put payoff − premium. Break-even = purchase price + premium.
topics.key: The premium is the cost of protection; upside remains if the share rises.
topics.classNotes: Class note: A protective put combines ownership of the underlying with a bought put. It creates a downside floor (before considering costs) while retaining upside participation; the premium is the cost of that protection.

topics.title: Bull call spread
topics.detail: Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call with the same expiry; expect a moderate rise.
topics.simple: The second call helps pay for the first, but limits how much you can make.
topics.example: Class example: buy 19,300 call for ₹150; sell 19,500 call for ₹70. Net debit ₹80; max loss ₹80; max gain ₹120; break-even ₹19,380.
points: Maximum gain = strike difference − net debit. Break-even = lower strike + net debit.
topics.key: The maximum loss is the net debit; maximum gain is capped.
topics.classNotes: Class note: The handwritten pages describe buying a lower-strike call and selling a higher-strike call. Net debit is the premium paid minus premium received; maximum loss is the net debit, maximum gain is strike difference minus net debit, and break-even is lower strike plus net debit.

topics.title: Bear put spread
topics.detail: Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put with the same expiry; expect a moderate fall.
topics.simple: The second put reduces the cost of protection/profit opportunity but caps the gain.
topics.example: Class example: buy 19,000 put for ₹120; sell 18,800 put for ₹80. Net debit ₹40; max loss ₹40; max gain ₹160; break-even ₹18,960.
points: Maximum gain = strike difference − net debit. Break-even = higher strike − net debit.
topics.key: The maximum loss is the net debit; maximum gain is capped.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put. Net debit is premium paid minus premium received; maximum loss is the net debit, maximum gain is strike difference minus net debit, and break-even is higher strike minus net debit.

topics.title: Commodity markets
topics.detail: Commodity markets trade movable, tangible goods such as metals, energy and agricultural products.
topics.simple: These are markets for physical goods, not company shares or bonds.
topics.example: A farmer worries wheat prices may fall before harvest; a food producer worries prices may rise before buying supplies.
points: The slides classify commodities as perishable/non-perishable and consumable/non-consumable.
topics.key: Quality, location, storage, transport and perishability can affect commodity prices.

topics.title: Commodity derivatives
topics.detail: Commodity derivatives are contracts whose value depends on a physical commodity's price.
topics.simple: They help farmers, producers and users manage uncertainty about future commodity prices.
topics.example: A farmer sells wheat futures to reduce the risk of a price fall before harvest. A buyer can hedge against prices rising.
points: The slides cover futures, options, forwards and swaps. Participants include hedgers, speculators and arbitrageurs.
topics.key: Hedging reduces existing price exposure; speculation seeks profit from price movement; arbitrage exploits price differences.
topics.classNotes: Class note: The lecture examples calculate futures gains/losses for long and short positions, include brokerage/transaction costs, and use simultaneous cash-market and futures positions to demonstrate hedging. A hedge is intended to reduce exposure to an adverse price movement, not guarantee a profit.

topics.title: Commodity exchanges
topics.detail: Commodity exchanges provide organised platforms for trading standardised commodity contracts.
topics.simple: They bring buyers and sellers together under common contract and delivery rules.
topics.example: NCDEX is described as agriculture-focused; MCX covers bullion, energy and metals among other commodity groups.
points: The slides also name TOCOM, Dalian Commodity Exchange, Shanghai Futures Exchange and CME Group.
topics.key: Physical delivery can require warehouses, transport and quality checks; storage, perishability and location matter.

quizzes.question: A company issues fresh shares to investors to raise new capital. Where does this transaction take place?
quizzes.explanation: The primary market is where securities are issued for the first time and the issuer raises funds. Once those securities are traded between investors, the trades occur in the secondary market.

quizzes.question: Which statement best explains why a rise in call-money rates can indicate tighter short-term liquidity?
choices: Banks have more surplus funds to lend overnight
Immediate/very short-term funds are becoming scarcer relative to demand
Long-term corporate bonds have become risk-free
Equity market turnover must have increased
quizzes.explanation: Call money is very short-term borrowing and lending. When demand for immediate funds is high relative to available supply, the rate can rise. It is a liquidity signal, not proof by itself of a wider market event.

quizzes.question: A share is trading at ₹4,400. An investor places a buy limit order at ₹4,300. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: It can execute only at ₹4,300 or lower, and may remain unfilled
It triggers a buy only after the price rises above ₹4,300
It guarantees the investor will buy exactly at ₹4,300
quizzes.explanation: A buy limit sets the maximum price the investor is willing to pay. If the market does not reach ₹4,300 or lower, the order may not execute. A limit controls price, not execution certainty.

quizzes.question: A mutual fund has investments worth ₹12,00,000, other assets of ₹50,000, liabilities of ₹30,000 and 1,00,000 units outstanding. What is its NAV per unit?
quizzes.explanation: Net assets = ₹12,00,000 + ₹50,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹12,20,000. NAV per unit = ₹12,20,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹12.20. Always subtract liabilities before dividing by units.

quizzes.question: A ₹1,000 face-value bond pays a 9% annual coupon for five years. If the required annual yield is 10%, which is the closest fair value?
quizzes.explanation: Annual coupon = ₹90. Price = 90/(1.10) + 90/(1.10)² + 90/(1.10)³ + 90/(1.10)⁴ + 1,090/(1.10)⁵ ≈ ₹962.07. Because the coupon rate (9%) is below the required yield (10%), the bond trades at a discount.

quizzes.question: A bond has a face value of ₹1,000, annual coupon of ₹80 and current market price of ₹950. Which statement is correct about its current yield?
quizzes.explanation: Current yield = annual coupon ÷ current market price × 100 = 80/950 × 100 ≈ 8.42%. It does not include the capital gain or loss that may occur by maturity, so it is not the same as YTM.

quizzes.question: You have 12 monthly active-return observations (fund return minus benchmark return). After calculating their sample standard deviation, how do you annualise monthly tracking error using the class method?
quizzes.explanation: The class notes calculate the standard deviation of monthly active returns and annualise it by multiplying by √12. This assumes monthly observations are suitable for the standard annualisation convention used in the lecture.

quizzes.question: A trader goes long 1,000 futures units at ₹269.80 and closes at ₹275.00. The notes assume a transaction cost of ₹0.20 per unit for the relevant round-trip calculation. What is the net gain under that class illustration?
quizzes.explanation: Gross gain per unit = ₹275.00 − ₹269.80 = ₹5.20. Less ₹0.20 transaction cost = ₹5.00 net per unit. Net gain = ₹5 × 1,000 = ₹5,000. Follow the cost assumption stated in the question; do not deduct the same cost twice.

quizzes.question: A bond has modified duration of 4.2. Using the duration approximation, what is the estimated percentage price change if its yield rises by 0.50 percentage points?
quizzes.explanation: Approximate % price change ≈ − modified duration × change in yield. The yield change is +0.005, so −4.2 × 0.005 = −0.021, or approximately −2.10%. The negative sign captures the inverse price–yield relationship.

quizzes.question: An investor owns a share and buys a put option on that same share. Which position is created, and what is its main trade-off?
choices: Covered call; upside is capped and no downside floor exists
Protective put; downside is limited by the put's protection, but the premium is a cost
Bull call spread; both upside and downside are unlimited
Bear put spread; the investor has no exposure to the underlying
quizzes.explanation: A protective put = long underlying + long put. If the share falls below the put strike, the put gains value and cushions the loss. The investor pays a premium for this protection; upside in the share is retained, before costs.
